items.title: Gen X’s $2.3 trillion caregiving curse: I’m the sister from John Mulaney’s SNL skit and I did the math
items.summary:
On Saturday Night Live this weekend, John Mulaney sold America its oldest elder-care product. “Sister,” his pitchman explains, is a live-in, 24/7 caregiver who is “completely free, and also your sister.” Mikey Day’s Dr. Grant, author of Not It! A Son’s Guide to Elder Care, explains how it works: years of internalized sexism have convinced her that caring for Mom and Dad is her job and somehow not yours. The best part, another brother adds, is that the parents drew up the will before she moved in, so you still get half the house she’s deep cleaning. Within a day, the sketch had 2 million views on YouTube, and women all over the country were sending it to their brothers.

The joke lands because it isn’t one, particularly the part about finances. It’s impossible to create or maintain wealth while caregiving.

I have no brothers, but I’m the sister. For the last 14 years (and several years in the past) I have been my parents’ full-time caregiver, without pay. My father passed away in 2022 and somehow the work increased taking care of one parent. I clean up after her at every meal, several times a day. I manage her medications, take her to specialists, deal with her insurers, rub lotion on her feet, run her errands, log in for her on some device several times a day. I’m a columnist, and my work has shrunk to fit around her care: missed meetings, moved deadlines, the same explanation of her health given again to every editor and board I work with. Each year I earn less than I would have, and each of those years goes into my Social Security record as a smaller number, almost a…
items.t: Gen X’s $2.3 trillion caregiving curse: I’m the sister from John Mulaney’s SNL skit and I did the math

items.title: Grand Theft Auto made crime a game. AI is doing the same for hacking
items.summary:
Fans have waited 13 years for Grand Theft Auto VI. The wait for GTA V’s sequel dragged on through so many delays that it became a meme. When a game takes that long, you’d expect it to feel dated on arrival. But when GTA VI finally arrived this week, the opposite thing happened. The real world has started to look a lot like the game.

Six days before the launch, the FBI issued a FLASH warning about ARTEX, an open-source tool that lets AI agents carry out an intrusion “at machine speed, from reconnaissance through data exfiltration.” Some attacks reached privileged access in under three hours. The GitHub repository has since been taken down, but copies are still out there, and it has already been used against banks, government agencies, and tech companies. Skill, time, and money used to separate a bored teenager from a professional crew. Now a bored teenager with AI can operate like one.

Rockstar knows what a bored teenager can do. In 2022, a 17-year-old broke into the company and leaked early GTA VI footage from a hotel room, using an Amazon Fire Stick and a phone. That took some serious skills and marked the last time anyone would need them. Rockstar spent 13 years building a game that feels like real life. In the same stretch, real life took on the rules of the game. AI turned the hacking craft into a criminal loop. You pick a target, try, fail, try again, at almost no cost, with the push of a button, from your couch. While developing the latest GTA took more than a decade, reality caught up in a fraction of that.

That shift left defenses behind, because they were built…
items.t: Grand Theft Auto made crime a game. AI is doing the same for hacking

items.title: SNL’s viral ‘Sister’ sketch asks why pay for elder care when a daughter does it free — a home health aide runs about $6,688 a month
items.summary:
A “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “ Sister ” has gone viral. The premise was simple: Why pay for professional care for an aging parent when a daughter can do it for free?

The clip, which first aired on Nov. 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families.

According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 63 million Americans provide ongoing care to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade. About 61% of these caregivers are women.

As researchers who study aging , long-term care and financial security, we’ve found that those who become caregivers initially have better health and financial status than noncaregivers. But they then experience relatively worse health and financial decline over time compared with their noncaregiving counterparts.

While societal gender expectations help explain why daughters often assume the bulk of caregiving responsibilities, government policies have also determined how much care families must provide.

Medicare doesn’t cover long-term care 

One of the most consequential features of America’s long-term care system is that Medicare, the federal health insurance program covering most adults 65 and older, generally does not pay for ongoing care and assistance with everyday activities.

Medicare covers hospitalizations, physician visits and certain home health services. However, those who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, preparing meals…
items.t: SNL’s viral ‘Sister’ sketch asks why pay for elder care when a daughter does it free — a home health aide runs about $6,688 a month

items.title: Trump, Putin and Xi signed onto a 1985 Reagan-Gorbachev nuclear line in 90 minutes of talks — Ukraine didn’t even come up by name
items.summary:
It was touted as a history-making summit of the year. Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping sat down on Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, on the sideline of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit , for the first such trilateral meeting of the three leaders.

Going into the talks, the trio had much to dicuss: the ongoing war in Ukraine , Middle East conflict and the march of artificial intelligence technology chief among them.

But what did 90 minutes of conversation deliver?

As an expert on U.S.-China relations at Harvard Kennedy School , I saw a lot of style, but less substance.

What were the key takeaways from the meeting? 

The first thing to pay attention to is the symbolism of the occasion. And so much of what was presented in Shenzhen was about the body language of the three men, their interactions and what that may indicate in regards to how they view themselves in a potentially new global order.

And this was on show even before the leaders sat down. At the beginning of the trip, when Trump landed in Shenzhen, he was met by Xi . Meeting a foreign leader at the airport is seen as a special honor bestowed by the Chinese president.

And then came a hug – that really was unprecedented. I haven’t seen the general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party hug anyone before – certainly not his Politburo comrades.

It was all choreographed, of course. But it continued into the summit itself. The picture of a big table with Trump, Putin and Xi there is also symbolic. And look who was in the middle: Xi. Here we have China presenting as the “Middle…
items.t: Trump, Putin and Xi signed onto a 1985 Reagan-Gorbachev nuclear line in 90 minutes of talks — Ukraine didn’t even come up by name

items.title: Data centers went from about 3% of Oregon’s electricity use to about 23% in a decade — and account for 96% of its power-sales growth since 2020
items.summary:
It takes a lot of electricity to power the sprawling computing campuses undergirding the artificial intelligence boom: a lot for servers, a lot for cooling the chips, a lot for networking, and a bit for keeping the actual lights on. Yet translating “a lot” to real numbers pinned to individual facilities requires usage data, something that data-center operators are loath to disclose.

A Harvard-led study published this week in Nature Sustainability gets us closer to these numbers. Researchers extracted locations and building footprints for as many U.S. hyperscale data centers as possible, ultimately cataloguing 403 of the warehouse-sized facilities across the country. Translating power capacity to theoretical electricity usage, the authors estimated these facilities gobble up roughly 82 terawatt-hours of electricity annually, the equivalent of nearly 8 million homes. They suggest this electricity is associated with about 26 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions.

The 82-TWh estimate corresponds to about 2 percent of U.S. electricity. Though noteworthy in its own right, that figure shrouds high state-to-state variability, with many states boasting data-center electricity shares in the double digits. When viewed as a fraction of the retail electricity sales reported to the Energy Information Administration (EIA) in 2024, Oregon’s studied data centers used the equivalent of 18.6 percent of the electricity sold in the state. In Virginia and Iowa, data centers consumed 15.5 and 13.1 percent, respectively.

While data-center electricity consumption remains a national…
items.t: Data centers went from about 3% of Oregon’s electricity use to about 23% in a decade — and account for 96% of its power-sales growth since 2020

items.title: Senate passes first-ever prediction market bill as Democrats turn up heat on upstart industry
items.summary:
Prediction markets are facing new limits on Capitol Hill. The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would bar platforms from offering contracts tied to terrorism, assassination, an individual’s death, war or U.S. military operations–the first legislation targeting the burgeoning industry to clear either chamber of Congress.

Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and John Curtis (R-Utah) introduced the bill, formally called the DEATH BETS Act, to prevent exchanges and clearinghouses overseen by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission from offering or processing those contracts. It would also ban contracts whose outcomes are reasonably expected to depend mainly on someone’s death, even if the wording does not mention death. 

The bill passed the Senate by a voice vote and must still pass the House before heading to the president’s desk.

“They are offered with no regard for national security and in far too many cases, even basic morality,” Schiff said on the Senate floor. “These markets are operating in a wild West, desperately in need of regulation and guardrails.”

As platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket have grown in prominence over the past two years, they have offered contracts on seemingly anything , drawing scrutiny over bets tied to war, violence or human suffering. They have also raised concerns about insider trading, as users can trade without publicly revealing their identities, making it harder for outsiders to spot potential conflicts of interest.

Several cases have drawn politicians’ attention to these issues. One involved a Polymarket trader who made more than…
items.t: Senate passes first-ever prediction market bill as Democrats turn up heat on upstart industry

items.title: Anthropic’s stock is now just 15 cents above its IPO price, a stunning reversal of its first day pop
items.summary:
Anthropic’s stock is on the brink of falling below its initial public offering price on Friday, erasing the gains made a day earlier during the AI company’s blockbuster Wall Street debut .

Shares in the buzzy AI lab traded as low as $83.15 on Friday, down more than 14% on their second day of trading. The shares are down more than 25% from the intraday high of $115.10 they achieved on Thursday, the first day the stock traded.

The current price puts the stock just a hair above its IPO price of $83, at which Anthropic was valued at approximately $1.5 trillion.

The retreat in the stock comes amid broader weakness in technology shares, as investors reassess valuations across the board. Problems at AI giant Nvidia and the results of the midterm elections have also worried the markets in recent weeks.

Anthropic’s decline marks a sharp reversal from Thursday’s opening session, when Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, 34% above the IPO price, and then surged even higher, briefly pushing the company’s market capitalization above $2 trillion. The stock quickly pared back those gains though to close at $97.17, still 17% above its offering price and an impressive first day.

Anthropic’s IPO was one of the largest in history, with the company raising approximately $91 billion through the share sale (including a 147 million-share over-allotment sold by the deal’s underwriters on Friday), plus an additional $26 billion private placement. All told, Anthropic raised more than $115 billion in the offering—capital that will be vital to its efforts to stay ahead in the AI race, regardless…
items.t: Anthropic stock teeters close to IPO price in second day of trading

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.summary:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

Continue reading...
items.t: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers

items.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
items.summary:
Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism

It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

items.t: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier

items.title: Warby Parker is betting its next chapter on smart glasses people actually want to wear
items.summary:
Warby Parker is one of the clear winners of the 2010s-era direct-to-consumer (DTC) wave. It and other upstart digital-first brands like Allbirds shoes, Away luggage, and Casper mattresses used e-commerce savvy to cut out middlemen like wholesalers, upending their industries and selling straight to shoppers.

While many of its peers from that era have struggled or shut down, Warby Parker retains an empire of 360 stores; its revenue increased 10% to $245 million in its most recent quarter. Still, the eyewear company is grappling with soft growth in new active customers—only 3.4% last quarter—and a sluggish eyewear market overall.

In search of its next big growth engine, Warby Parker is planting its flag in the promising but still tiny market for smart glasses, teaming up with Google. The tech behemoth, along with partner Samsung , will provide the AI technology behind the glasses, including a high-resolution display tucked inside one lens that wearers can control with a wristband or watch.

For Warby Parker, whose own innovations have included a virtual try-on and features that enable customers to choose glasses from home, the partnership could bolster its tech-forward reputation, tapping its strengths in design and retail to win eyeglass buyers of the future. 

“Glasses are the original wearable, right?” says Warby Parker cofounder and co-CEO Neil Blumenthal on Fortune ’s Behind the Business YouTube series. “The combination of form and function is something we can bring to this new category and create something that has a ton of technology in it.”

items.title: The Altruists review – two of TV’s best actors light up this chaotic crypto tale
items.summary:
Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle play the FTX founders behind ‘the greatest fraud ever committed’ in the US. It’s a mind-boggling story – just make sure you don’t miss a single moment

What happens when you put really stupid clever people in charge of the world? Not as presidents (they currently trend mostly towards the merely stupid) or prime ministers (generally neither really stupid nor really clever), but in charge of the real world, which is to say the online world, the one that really governs us? We are watching that play out day by day, but if you have enough slack left in your dread-system, a cortisol spike yet to execute, why not add a warning from history to your consumption of horrors?

Welcome to The Altruists, a breakneck breakdown of the brief career of Sam Bankman-Fried (played by Anthony Boyle) who, with his on-off girlfriend Caroline Ellison (played by Julia Garner), set up the cryptocurrency exchange FTX with the belief that it would revolutionise finance and – as the increasingly absurd/dishonest/knowingly satirical Silicon Valley mantra has it – make the world a better place. A very few years later, FTX – worth $36bn (£27bn) at its peak – collapsed and in 2023 the pair were convicted of various charges deriving from what the trial judge called “the greatest financial fraud ever perpetrated in this country”. Ellison was sentenced to two years in prison after testifying against Bankman-Fried. Bankman-Fried is serving 25 years and was ordered to forfeit $11bn (£8.3bn). He says he is innocent and is applying to the supreme court to review his…
items.t: The Altruists review – two of TV’s best actors light up this chaotic crypto tale

items.title: Grade I interiors, gold bars, cost fears: Bank of England faces headache over £160m revamp
items.summary:
UK central bank will want to avoid echoes of expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that led to Trump clash

Andrew Bailey may spend his days closely watching developments in the strait of Hormuz or US stock markets for signs of shocks to the global economy – but the Bank of England’s governor has a £160m problem brewing much closer to home.

A secretive major revamp of the Bank’s historic headquarters in the heart of London’s Square Mile presents a huge test of Bailey’s project management skills. The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera.

items.title: Flexibility more important to jobseekers than pay, global survey finds
items.summary:
A poll of more than 40,000 workers found that a better work-life balance was the main reason people consider leaving their jobs

Work-life balance has become the leading reason why workers consider leaving their jobs, according to a new global workforce survey, as flexibility is valued more than a higher salary despite the cost of living crisis.

A poll of more than 40,000 global workers found that the top reasons for seeking a new role were better balance between professional and private lives, more flexibility over working schedules or remote working opportunities.

items.t: Flexibility more important to jobseekers than pay, global survey finds

items.title: Weight-loss drugs used in nearly one in 10 homes in Great Britain, study finds
items.summary:
About 2.6m adults are taking the drugs, fuelled by the regulator’s approval of the pill versions and a rise in male users

At least one person is taking weight-loss drugs in 8.5% of households in Great Britain, according to research, meaning there are more homes with GLP-1 users than those containing vegetarians and pescatarians combined.

About 2.6 million adults were using weight-loss medication in August, a rise of about 700,000 people since February, according to a survey by Worldpanel by Numerator.

items.t: Weight-loss drugs used in nearly one in 10 homes in Great Britain, study finds

Elon Musk denied being Maga on Wednesday, despite aligning himself intensely with Donald Trump’s “Make America great again” movement since 2024.

“I’m not Maga,” the world’s richest person told the New York Times Dealbook summit, which he attended via video call from China, where he is one of several US business leaders who have accompanied Trump on his trip to Asia.

items.title: Leaseholders in England and Wales to have ground rent capped in 2028
items.summary:
Housing minister hails ‘historic moment’ as he publishes bill to eventually ban almost all new leasehold properties

Leaseholders in England and Wales will have their ground rent capped in 2028, the housing minister has said as he publishes a bill that will eventually ban virtually all new leasehold properties.

Matthew Pennycook will introduce the government’s leasehold reform bill on Thursday, including measures to cap charges, end the sale of new leasehold flats and make it easier to extend and buy out leases.
